facts.fact_text: The case concerns the dispersal by the police of a demonstration organised by a political party.
According to police reports, at about 4.40 p.m. on 3 June 2010, the applicants joined the front lines of demonstrators.
As the demonstrators continued to march despite another warning, the police dispersed them by using water cannon and tear gas.
A number of demonstrators were carrying wooden sticks during the demonstration on 3 June 2010.
A number of demonstrators were carrying flags of the PKK (Workers' Party of Kurdistan) during the demonstration on 3 June 2010.
As the demonstrators continued to march despite another warning, the police dispersed them by using water cannon and tear gas.
During the first moments of the police intervention on 3 June 2010, the second applicant fell to the ground and sustained injuries to her hip.
The second applicant was subsequently taken to the Silopi Public Hospital after sustaining injuries during the police intervention on 3 June 2010.
A medical report drawn up by the Silopi Public Hospital at 5.25 p.m. on 3 June 2010 mentioned that the second applicant had a fractured neck of femur (a type of hip fracture).
The fractured neck of femur sustained by the second applicant could not be treated by a simple medical procedure.
The second applicant was subsequently transported to a private hospital in Ankara, where she was operated on 3 June 2010.
The second applicant was discharged from the private hospital in Ankara on 11 June 2010.
After being discharged from hospital on 11 June 2010, the second applicant received physiotherapy owing to her inability to walk.
The second applicant was prescribed several consecutive periods of sick leave lasting until 24 March 2011.
A medical report from 2014 indicated that the second applicant was able to walk with crutches.
In her submissions to the Court, the second applicant stated that she was still receiving treatment for her injury.
The Government provided the Court with several video recordings made by the police during the events of 3 June 2010.
The video footage shows the second applicant in the front lines of demonstrators immediately before the spraying of pressurised water towards that area.
Although it is impossible to see clearly the exact moment when the second applicant fell, the video footage shows that she was on the ground immediately after the first round of water spraying.
The video footage shows that the second applicant attempted to stand up after her fall but was unable to do so.
The video footage shows that pressurised water was sprayed more than once during the police intervention on 3 June 2010.
The video footage shows that the traffic on the road in question was not stopped until the demonstrators began heading towards the BDP bus.
The video footage shows that the police intervention began less than two minutes after the applicants joined the front lines of demonstrators.
The relevant domestic law in respect of freedom of assembly is set out in Oya Ataman v. Turkey (no. 74552/01, §§ 13-15, ECHR 2006-XIV).

At the material time, section 10 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) required that in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration is planned must be informed, during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting, by a notice containing the signature of all the members of the organising committee.
Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), as in force at the material time, prohibited demonstrations and processions on public streets and highways.

Section 24 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) provided that demonstrations and processions which did not comply with the provisions of the Act would be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators had been warned.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, when faced with resistance in the performance of their duties, the police may use force for the purpose of, and to the extent necessary for, breaking down such resistance.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, the use of force means recourse to physical and material force and weaponry in order to immobilise those resisting the police, in a graduated manner depending on the nature and degree of resistance.
Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, the term 'material force' is defined as including handcuffs, truncheons, pressurised water and tear gas.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, a warning is required before using force; however, depending on the nature and degree of resistance, it may also be possible to use force without any warning.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, the police determine the equipment and the degree of force to be used, and where the action is taken against a group, that determination is made by the supervisor of the intervening unit.

Article 25 of the Directive of 30 December 1982 on the rapid reaction forces (Polis Çevik Kuvvet Yönetmeliği) lays down the principles governing the supervision, control and intervention of those forces during demonstrations, as summarised in Abdullah Yaşa and Others v. The chief inspectors' report noted that officials had expressed concerns that if the police did not intervene, the number of participants might increase, rendering it impossible to intervene.
The chief inspectors' report referred to concerns about possible provocative acts and serious incidents targeting the military barracks situated further along the road taken by the demonstrators.
The chief inspectors' report mentioned that the police had warned the protestors many times that the demonstration was unlawful and had ordered them to disperse.

The chief inspectors' report stated that as the crowd had not stopped advancing towards the police, the police had used water cannon and tear gas, prompted by concerns that it would become impossible to intervene if the crowd reached the police barricade.
The chief inspectors' report stated that the police intervention had lasted eight to ten seconds and that pressurised water had been sprayed only once.

The chief inspectors' report stated that there was nothing to indicate that the members of parliament had been targeted by the police officers, and that it was pure coincidence that the second applicant had been hit by water (tamamen tesadüfen suya hedef olduğu).
The chief inspectors' report stated that the injury sustained by the second applicant had been the result of her falling awkwardly (biçimsiz bir şekilde) owing to physical weakness.
The chief inspectors' report noted that the other demonstrators who had been hit by the same pressurised water had not been injured.

The chief inspectors' report found that the police had intervened at the right moment, given that there had been more than three thousand demonstrators and that their number could have reached ten thousand at any moment.
The chief inspectors' report found that there had been no serious injuries apart from that of the second applicant.
The chief inspectors' report concluded that the intervention had been carried out in such a manner as to cause the least possible damage.
